div.p: Each PersonalRelationship resource records a single, unidirectional relationship between two individuals. If the inverse relationship also needs to be recorded, it is represented by a separate PersonalRelationship resource. Properties such as confidence, period, and asserter are recorded independently and can differ between the two directions.

Some relationship types imply an inverse relationship, but do not determine its most specific type. For example, "father of" implies "child of", but does not establish whether the child is a son or daughter. Likewise, "child of" implies "parent of", but not specifically mother or father. Recording one direction does not automatically create a PersonalRelationship resource for the inverse direction.
The family relationship examples use Patient resources for Jane, John, and Mary, and four separate PersonalRelationship resources:

li.a: Mary (source) is the daughter (relationshipType) of Jane (target).
Jane (source) is the mother (relationshipType) of Mary (target).
Mary (source) is the daughter (relationshipType) of John (target).
John (source) is the father (relationshipType) of Mary (target).

div.p: Each PersonalRelationship describes only one direction. The daughter and mother relationships between Mary and Jane are recorded explicitly, rather than relying on an inferred inverse. Confidence applies only to the relationship on which it is recorded; omitting it does not assert certainty.

The extended and blended families below are separate extensions of the simple family above, rather than one combined family. They reuse the Patient resources for Jane, John, and Mary. The foster home is a separate household. All additional relationships explicitly record certain confidence. Each table entry links to an individual PersonalRelationship resource, including a separate resource for the inverse direction.
Jane's parents are Alice and Robert. Jane and John also have a son, Peter, who is Mary's brother; Mary is Peter's sister. Alice and Robert are the maternal grandparents of both Mary and Peter.

In addition to the parent/child relationships in the simple family, the following resources explicitly record the relationships between the grandparents and their daughter Jane, the grandparents and each grandchild, Peter and his parents, and the two siblings. A grandparent relationship is recorded directly rather than relying on an application to derive it by traversing parent/child relationships.

In this extension of the simple family, Tom is John's biological son from an earlier relationship and Jane's stepson. Jane is Tom's stepmother. Tom and Mary share John as their biological father, so they are half-siblings, not step-siblings. Anna is the adopted daughter of both Jane and John. Mary and Tom are Anna's siblings within the adoptive family.

The relationship types distinguish biological, step, and adoptive parent/child relationships. The generic sister and brother codes used for Anna's sibling relationships do not assert biological kinship. Each relationship is recorded separately, rather than assuming that a relationship with a parent automatically creates relationships with the other children.

In a separate household, Emma and David are foster parents of Leo. Leo was placed with them from 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-31. Each of the four PersonalRelationship resources below records that interval in period, with certain confidence.

The foster relationship does not by itself assert biological parentage or legal guardianship. The placement has ended, but the relationships can still be retained as historical information. These resources describe the familial relationships, not any care activities performed by Emma or David.
